texts.setting.compatibilityrules.about: Ruffle includes fixes for specific known games on specific sites. They rewrite some addresses and patch some behaviour so those games work. Ruffle's own players turn them on. This core keeps them off by default, so that the movie behaves exactly as it was published and a recording is of the movie alone. Turn them on if a known game does not run otherwise. The choice is part of the run, so a movie recorded with them on must be played back with them on.
texts.setting.defaultfont.about: Draws text in Ruffle's built-in font when the movie asks for a system font it did not include. With this off, such text is not drawn at all. That is what a computer without the font would have shown, but it usually just means missing menus. It changes the picture only.
texts.setting.fps.about: How many times a second the machine advances, which is also how often the input can change. 0 means the movie's own frame rate, which is what a Flash player uses and what almost everything needs. One frame here is then one frame of the movie, and when the movie changes its rate from ActionScript, the frames here change with it. With a higher number the movie still runs at its own speed. Nothing plays faster, but each movie frame becomes several frames here, so a click, a key press or a mouse move can be placed between two movie frames. That makes a game easier to control when it reads the mouse in the middle of its frame or runs by elapsed time. The cost is more frames to draw, more rows of input and a larger file. A multiple of the movie's rate (30 to 60 or 120) keeps the movie frames evenly spaced. Any other number also works. It is part of the machine, so a movie recorded at one rate must be played back at the same one.
texts.setting.loadbehavior.about: What a movie sees while another SWF it loads is still arriving. 'streaming' lets the loaded movie start before it is complete and reports its progress as it grows, like a real player on a real connection. 'delayed' holds the loaded movie back until all of it has arrived. 'blocking' stops everything until the load is finished, so the movie never sees a partial load. Files arrive at once from disk here, so in practice this mostly decides whether a loading animation gets to play.
texts.setting.pageurl.about: The address of the web page the movie is told it is embedded in. This is a different thing from where the movie file came from. ActionScript reads it as Security.pageDomain, and a game that checks its site sometimes checks this address and not the movie's own. Leave it empty unless a game refuses to start with Spoofed URL alone. In that case set both to the same site.
texts.setting.playerruntime.about: Flash Player or Adobe AIR. AIR has everything Flash Player has plus file and system functions, and content made for it checks which of the two it runs on. Almost every .swf from the web is Flash Player content. Change this only for a movie that was packaged as an AIR application.
texts.setting.playerversion.about: Which Flash Player version the movie is told it runs on. 0 means the version the SWF file asks for, which is right for almost everything. Raise it when a movie refuses to run on the version it finds. Lower it when a movie takes a code path for a newer player that does not work. Movies of this age often behave differently depending on the player version. It changes what the movie does, so a movie recorded at one version must be played back at the same one.
texts.setting.quality.about: How smoothly shapes are drawn. This is Flash's own Stage.quality setting, with Ruffle's higher levels added. 'high' is Flash's default and what movies were made for. 'low' turns anti-aliasing off, which is faster and is sometimes how a movie was really seen. The higher levels draw at a finer resolution and cost graphics time. It changes the picture only. The game does not depend on it, and a movie can change the quality itself while it runs.
texts.setting.renderer.about: Where Ruffle's picture is drawn. Both choices use the same Ruffle renderer and differ only in which OpenGL does the drawing. 'opengl-hw' sends the drawing out of the sandbox to your computer's graphics card. It is the default because drawing in software is too slow to play (about 0.87 frames a second was measured on New Star Soccer). The picture is then NOT guaranteed to be the same on every computer, because it comes from your graphics driver. The game itself still runs the same, with one exception: when a movie draws its own display into a bitmap and reads it back (BitmapData.draw), the picture does reach the game. This choice needs a Chimera built with the GPU bridge, and without one the core refuses to start. 'software' draws inside the sandbox with Mesa's software renderer, which is part of the core. The picture is then the same on every computer and in every replay. Choose it when a replay has to reproduce the picture exactly and the speed is acceptable. The software renderer cannot smooth edges, so it draws without anti-aliasing whatever the quality setting says.
texts.setting.spoofurl.about: The web address the movie is told it was loaded from. Left empty, the movie is loaded as file:///game.swf, like a local file. Many Flash games check this. Some refuse to start anywhere except their sponsor's site, some sign their requests against the page they came from, and files a movie loads by a relative name (a level, music, a scoreboard) are looked up against this address. Set it to the page the game was published on, for example https://www.kongregate.com/games/example, and those checks see what they expect. It does not change how the movie is emulated. It is one piece of text given to the player at load, so a movie recorded with one address must be played back with the same one.
texts.slot.assets.help: Everything the movie loads while it runs (with loadMovie, loadSound, loadVariables or URLLoader). These are more .swf files, images, sounds and data. Keep the names the movie asks for, because it looks for them next to itself. A movie that loads nothing needs nothing here.
